issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: Harold still remembers the night he was assaulted on his delivery route. It had been a typical evening, with the sun setting over the quiet suburban streets, when suddenly, out of nowhere, a stranger appeared and attacked him. The incident left Harold shaken, not just physically but also emotionally. As time passed, he found himself increasingly consumed by self-doubt, wondering if he could have done something to prevent the attack. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he had been careless or foolish, that somehow, it was all his fault. As these negative thoughts took hold, Harold began to change his behavior in ways that seemed small at first but soon became habits. He started working longer hours, taking on extra routes and deliveries, trying to keep himself busy with other things so he wouldn't have time to think about the attack. He also found solace in food, eating excessively as a way to manage his distress. His wife, Margaret, would often comment on how much more he was eating, but Harold just shrugged it off, saying he needed the energy for work. What frightened Harold most was the thought of being alone with his memories. If he allowed himself to think about the event, he was convinced that he wouldn't be able to handle it. He became adept at suppressing these thoughts, pushing them deep down whenever they began to surface. But this avoidance came at a cost. His relationships with Margaret and their friends began to suffer as Harold withdrew into his work and his own little world of avoidance. As the weeks turned into months, Harold's negative appraisals only intensified. He felt like he was losing his sense of purpose, that his whole worldview had been shattered by the assault. He couldn't trust himself to do the right thing anymore, and this self-doubt seeped into every aspect of his life. His busyness and overeating became coping mechanisms, ways to temporarily escape the crushing weight of these negative thoughts. Despite his best efforts, Harold couldn't shake off the feeling that he was living in a state of constant threat. He would see strangers on the street and immediately think of the attacker, his heart racing as he quickened his pace. Even the familiar routes he drove every day became potential sources of danger, each new face a possible threat. It was Margaret who finally encouraged Harold to seek help. She couldn't watch him continue down this path, eating more and more, working longer hours, and withdrawing further into himself. Harold knew she was right; he just didn't know how to stop the cycle. What brought him to therapy was the realization that he couldn't keep living like this, constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for the other shoe to drop. He hoped that somehow, someway, he could learn to let go of these negative thoughts and find a way back to himself. As Harold sat in the therapist's office, he looked like a man who had been running from his memories for far too long. His eyes were tired, his face lined with worry, but there was a glimmer of hope, a sense that maybe, just maybe, he could find a way to reclaim his life and learn to trust himself once more.
